To handle functions with local variables, we extend the environment model in a straightforward manner. Consider for example the function f_3 from section and its helper function square.
f_3_b f_3_b_example 456
def square(z): return z * z def f_3(x, y): a = 1 + x * y b = 1 - y return x * square(a) + y * b + a * b
f_3_b_example
print(f_3(3, 4))
As with simple functions, a call f_3(3, 4) creates a new environment, E1, beginning with a frame in which x and y, the parameters of f_3, are bound to the arguments 3 and 4, respectively. However, f_3 has declaration assignments for the local variables a and b, and subsequent references to the local variables need to refer to their values. To prepare for the evaluation of declaration assignments and their variables, the frame has bindings for a and b in addition to x and y. Before the the body of f_3 is evaluated, a and b do not refer to any values yet, we say they are unassigned. The evaluation of the assignments to a and b follows the rule for assignment in the previous section and thus modifies the frame so that a refers to 13, the result of evaluating 1 + x * y, and b refers to -3, the result of evaluating 1 - y. The remaining statement in the function body, return x * square(a) + y * b + a * b, contains the call square(a), which evaluates the body of square, return z * z, in a new environment, E2, beginning with a frame in which the parameter z refers to 13. The evaluation of the return expression of f_3 uses the result 169 and the values of the other variables in the environment E1 and computes 456 as the result of the function call f_3(3, 4).
